title: Continuation of the National Emergency With Respect to the Democratic Republic of the Congo
summary:
The White House has extended for another year the national emergency related to the situation in and around the Democratic Republic of the Congo, citing ongoing violence and instability that continue to threaten U.S. foreign policy interests.

First put in place in 2006 and updated in 2014, this emergency status keeps in place tools the U.S. uses to address those who fuel conflict and abuses, including targeted restrictions. The administration says the conditions that led to the original declaration have not improved enough to lift it. As required by law, the notice will be sent to Congress and published publicly.

Who stands to benefit? U.S. policymakers retain legal authority to act quickly against individuals and groups that drive violence or undermine regional stability. Regional partners and international organizations seeking peace and accountability may gain added leverage. Humanitarian and human rights advocates could see continued pressure on actors responsible for atrocities. Businesses and banks may also get clarity by maintaining a known set of rules they’ve already built compliance around.

Who could be negatively affected? People and entities designated under these authorities will continue to face restrictions, which can limit travel, access to funds, and business activities. Companies with ties to the region may encounter ongoing compliance costs, delays, or risk aversion from financial institutions. There can also be unintended spillover effects on ordinary Congolese if banks or suppliers pull back broadly to avoid risk, even when transactions are lawful.

In short, the U.S. is keeping its existing posture in place for another year, aiming to deter violence and support regional stability while accepting the trade-offs that come with extended emergency measures. The situation will be reviewed again next year.
